surface_forms: le charmant grand-duc héritier de Luxembourg

appraisal_events.evidence: « Ce que Mme de Guermantes croyait décevoir mon attente était, au contraire, ce qui […] sauvait ma soirée d’une déception complète » ; « J’avais commencé par la fée, dût-elle bientôt périr ; eux par la femme » ; « Sans le connaître eux-mêmes, ils me le procuraient comme eussent fait des laboureurs ou des matelots parlant de culture et de marées […] la beauté que personnellement je me chargeais d’en extraire. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator claims for himself the interpretive faculty the aristocrats lack: they own the names and the genealogies but cannot taste their poetry, while he alone converts their unfelt material into beauty and thereby rescues the evening. The passage is framed by this comparison and endorses it in the narrator's own voice.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Mais c’est un cousin d’Oriane ! » répété « presque à chaque nom qu’on prononçait » ; ces mots « semblaient avoir pour M. de Guermantes […] la même utilité que certaines épithètes commodes aux poètes latins, parce qu’elles leur fournissaient pour leurs hexamètres un dactyle ou un spondée » ; le monde aristocratique « réduisait sa grandeur nobiliaire à de simples supériorités domestiques, en vertu d’un enfantillage ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator reduces the duke's genealogical mastery to a mechanical verbal tic — metrical filler, or a signpost for a man lost in a wood — and assimilates his nobiliary pride to the petty domestic jealousies of bourgeois families. The same comic mechanism flattens the Turkish ambassadress's name-dropping, but the sustained ironic exposure falls on the duke himself.

status_effects.explanation: He ends the passage as the one competent reader of the names, extracting from Bréauté's ancestry the relics of Mme de Praslin and the duc de Berri; the elevation is real but qualified, since the fairy world he began with is conceded to be dying.
He is made locally ridiculous: his joyous rallying cry is treated as a prosodic convenience and his sense of nobility as childishness, so that he supplies poetry he cannot himself perceive.
The opening sentence turns her apology for the genealogies against her: she misjudges her guest, since precisely what she thought would bore him is what saved his evening.

ambiguities: The passage's most concentrated social humiliation falls on « l’ambassadrice de Turquie » — « la pauvre ambassadrice », « peu reçue », forced to admit « que son exemple était tiré d’animaux plus petits ». She is unnamed and absent from the reference sheet, so scope rules exclude her from characters_present; that episode is therefore represented only through the duke's side of the exchange in E2, and a clearly negative social_status effect for her is deliberately not recorded.

The diminishment of M. de Guermantes in E2 is narratorial and ironic only. Inside the salon the same reflex confirms his social security — he effortlessly deflates the ambassadress and defines the whole nobility by kinship to his wife — so the negative movement is placed on general_appraisal rather than social_status, which the passage leaves untouched or even reinforced.
